title: Why Japan's Prescription Rules Force Monthly Doctor Visits
hook: Japan has one of the world's most generous health insurance systems, but for a chronic prescription it still often means a clinic visit every single month.
target_query: why can't you get 90-day prescriptions in japan
free_section_html:
In Japan, patients managing a chronic condition like high blood pressure or diabetes usually cannot get more than about a month's supply of medication at once, and the prescription itself is only valid to fill within four days of being issued. There is no widespread American-style 90-day mail-order refill and no British-style repeat prescription that lets a patient collect months of medicine without seeing a doctor. To keep taking a daily pill, most people in Japan have to physically return to a clinic roughly every thirty days, get a new prescription form, then walk it to a pharmacy.

This is one of the quieter reasons Japan has the highest rate of doctor visits per person among wealthy nations. According to OECD health statistics, residents of Japan average somewhere around twelve to thirteen outpatient consultations a year, more than double the OECD average of roughly five or six. Some of that gap comes from short wait times and low copays, but a meaningful share comes from paperwork: refilling a prescription in Japan is not an administrative task a pharmacist can handle alone. It requires a physician's signature, which requires an appointment.

The rule has a legal and structural basis. Japan's pharmaceutical affairs law limits how long a dispensing prescription stays valid, and health insurance rules have historically discouraged unusually long supply intervals for many oral medications, with certain drug classes, including some sleep aids and anti-anxiety medications, restricted to even shorter windows. Pharmacists can advise and monitor, but they generally cannot authorize a refill on their own judgment the way a pharmacist in parts of the United States or Canada sometimes can.

The economics behind the monthly return visit

To understand why the system works this way, it helps to look at how Japanese clinics are actually paid. Under Japan's universal health insurance system, every medical service is priced on a national fee schedule set by the health ministry and revised roughly every two years. A clinic visit generates a specific reimbursement code: a first-visit fee (shoshinryō) for a new complaint, and a smaller revisit fee (saishinryō) for a follow-up. Add the fee for issuing a prescription, and a routine ten-minute check-in to renew blood pressure medication becomes a small, predictable stream of billable items.

Multiply that by tens of millions of patients with hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, or age-related conditions, and the monthly visit becomes a structural pillar of clinic revenue, not just a safety measure. Japan has an unusually high density of small, physician-owned clinics rather than large group practices, and many of these clinics depend on a steady rhythm of short, frequent visits to stay financially viable. A system that let patients disappear for three months at a time with a single prescription would remove a predictable and legally guaranteed source of income for exactly the kind of small practice that dominates Japanese primary care.

A regulatory relic: separating the prescriber from the pharmacy

Japan's prescription rules are also a legacy of a slower, deliberate reform. For most of the postwar era, Japanese doctors both prescribed and dispensed medication directly from their own clinics, profiting from the markup on drugs they sold. This gave doctors a financial incentive to over-prescribe, and by the 1990s policymakers pushed to separate prescribing from dispensing, a policy known as iyaku bungyō. Patients would now take a paper prescription to an independent pharmacy. The reform succeeded in reducing conflicts of interest and building an independent pharmacy sector, but it also hardened prescriptions into short-lived, single-use documents rather than standing authorizations. The four-day validity window and the informal caps on supply length were designed for an era when the point of a prescription was to be filled almost immediately, not banked for later use.

The quiet experiment nobody adopted at scale

Japan has not been blind to the burden this creates, especially as its population ages and the number of people managing multiple chronic conditions climbs. In discussions at the health ministry's Central Social Insurance Medical Council, officials have floated a narrower version of a repeat prescription, in which a doctor could designate a prescription as renewable a set number of times over a defined period, letting a pharmacist dispense a refill without a new physician visit for patients judged clinically stable. The idea has been debated for years and piloted in limited form, but adoption has stayed small. Physician groups have raised concerns that spacing out visits risks missing early signs of complications, worsening kidney function in a diabetic patient, for instance, or a blood pressure spike that a five-minute check-in might catch. There is also quieter resistance rooted in the clinic economics described above: fewer visits mean fewer billable encounters.

What patients actually pay, in money and time

The financial burden per visit is modest by international standards. Most working-age patients pay 30 percent of the cost out of pocket under Japan's insurance system, with lower rates for children and patients over 70, so a routine follow-up visit and prescription renewal often costs the patient the equivalent of a few thousand yen. That is far cheaper than an equivalent visit in an uninsured or high-deductible American context. But the time cost is real: a day off work, a wait in a clinic lobby, and a repeat of the same conversation about the same stable condition, month after month, year after year. For a country with a large elderly population and a shrinking pool of working-age caregivers who often accompany relatives to appointments, that recurring time cost adds up across the whole economy, not just the health budget.

Where the pressure is building

Two forces are pushing against the status quo. One is Japan's rapid aging: with a rising share of residents over 75, the volume of chronic-disease follow-ups needed just to keep the current model running is becoming difficult to staff, especially in rural areas losing physicians. The other is telemedicine, which expanded on a temporary basis during the COVID-19 pandemic and has since been kept in a limited, permanent form for certain follow-up visits, allowing some patients to renew a prescription through a video call rather than an in-person visit. Neither trend has yet dismantled the underlying rule that a doctor, not a pharmacist, must authorize each refill. But both are quietly testing whether Japan's famously frequent doctor visits are a reflection of the country's health needs, or a byproduct of how the system chose to get paid.
key_takeaways: Japanese prescriptions are typically valid to fill for only four days after issue and often cover no more than about a month of medication, unlike common 90-day refills elsewhere.
This rule is a major structural driver behind Japan's unusually high rate of doctor visits, roughly double the OECD average.
The rule traces back to a 1990s reform (iyaku bungyō) that separated prescribing from dispensing to curb doctors profiting from drug sales.
Small-scale 'repeat prescription' pilots that would let pharmacists renew stable patients' medication without a doctor visit have not been widely adopted.
Clinic reimbursement is billed per visit, giving Japan's many small, physician-owned clinics a financial incentive to keep monthly check-ins, not just a clinical one.

meta_description: Japan's four-day prescription rule and monthly refill system help explain why patients there see doctors more often than anywhere else on earth.
